title: Pipes and Redirection
summary: Save output into files with > and >>, and connect commands with the pipe |.
intro:
Until now, every answer went to the screen.
In this lesson you will send output into files, add lines to a diary, and connect commands like LEGO bricks with the pipe |.
There is a list of names in names.txt. Some names appear twice!
outro: Awesome! With >, >> and | you can combine small commands into powerful tools. This is the real superpower of the terminal.

steps.instruction: Save the output of ls into a file called files.txt (instead of showing it on the screen).
hints: The arrow > sends the output into a file instead of the screen.
steps.explain: Nothing appeared on the screen, because the output went into files.txt. Check with cat files.txt. Careful: > creates the file, or REPLACES everything in it if it already exists.

steps.instruction: Start a diary: write the line Day 1: I learned pipes into a file called diary.txt.
hints: Use echo to make the text and > to put it into the file.
Type: echo "Day 1: I learned pipes" > diary.txt
steps.explain: echo plus > is the fastest way to make a small text file.

steps.instruction: Add a second line, starting with Day 2:, to diary.txt. Don't lose Day 1!
hints: Two arrows >> mean 'append': add at the end of the file.
If you lost Day 1, just write it again with >, then add Day 2 with >>.
steps.explain: > replaces, >> adds. Mixing them up is a classic mistake that everybody makes once. Look at your diary with cat diary.txt.

steps.instruction: Sort the names in names.txt and remove the repeated ones, in ONE line.
hints: The pipe | (Shift + backslash on most keyboards) sends the output of one command into the next one. sort sorts lines, uniq removes repeats.
steps.explain: Your first pipe! uniq only removes repeats that are NEXT TO each other. That's why we sort first: then the same names end up side by side.

steps.instruction: Now save the sorted names without repeats into a file called unique_names.txt.
hints: Put > and the file name at the very end of the pipe.
steps.explain: Pipes and redirection work together like LEGO bricks: the data flows from left to right, and > catches it at the end.

steps.instruction: How many different names are there? Count them with a pipe.
hints: Add one more brick at the end: | wc -l
steps.explain: 6 different names! One more secret: error messages travel in a different stream, called stderr, so > does not catch them. Use 2> to save errors, for example: ls nothing 2> errors.txt
